title: The Path to the Head Is the Heart
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that schools, whose unique job is building students' minds, must first win the student's heart, because mastery requires both doing the work and doing it with care. Carrot-and-stick systems can coerce behavior but not care, so they yield middling returns. He grounds this in Ericsson's deliberate practice, noting that beneath deliberate practice lies the enlisted will. He then distinguishes engagement, a during-task immersion state, from motivation, the genuine desire to do a thing with care, and argues motivation is the sturdier target for teachers. Rather than leaning on Self-Determination Theory, he locates the root of care in five key beliefs, which he presents as a practical, explanatory framework linking theory to classroom action.
points: Mastery needs work done with care, and because rewards and punishments cannot coerce care, systems built on them stall at middling results.
Care is the potential energy beneath deliberate practice: students must want to identify sub-skills, give full effort and seek feedback before those habits can function.
Engagement is fragile and easily outcompeted by algorithmic feeds, so Stuart prioritizes motivation, which can carry students to and through tasks when engagement fails.
He roots motivation in five key beliefs rather than Self-Determination Theory, claiming very different classrooms succeed by sending the same signals to student hearts.
Good practitioner theory should explain what you see and carry practical implications, giving teachers a grid for analyzing problems and acting on solutions.
quotes: A person who does a thing — even does it well — is not necessarily a person who cares about what they’ve done. Instead, they can be a person who is driven by their care for the carrots or the sticks.

In other words, beneath deliberate practice — beneath the kind of work that optimally advances mastery — is care, is the enlisted will. Care is to mastery potential energy in the classroom as the sun is to potential energy on the earth.
So engagement is something that can get you through a task, but motivation is something that gets you to a task. And, when engagement wanes, motivation is what can get you back to it.
In other words, engagement is a worthy object of study for a teacher, but it’s not as resilient as motivation. It’s a Thoroughbred racehorse — fast and sexy, but fragile and with limited use cases.
When the heart is all set, the mind is primed for development. And understanding the five key beliefs can help you get the heart set in all kinds of settings.
But what I do believe very strongly is that when we rely on carrot/stick combos to get students to do work, we shouldn’t be surprise to see middling returns on the hard work we do in our classroom.
